title: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. • Отслеживаете
text: NODA AI went from a $10M contract to orchestrate drone swarms for one program (LUCAS) to a $100M contract to scale that same layer across the Joint Force — in roughly a month. That's not typical, and it's not just a good sales quarter. A single-program pilot and an enterprise-wide deployment are different technical problems. The pilot has to prove the orchestration works for one customer's platforms, one mission set, one integration point. The enterprise version has to work when the next platform added wasn't in the original design — different manufacturer, different data model, different failure mode — without a rewrite. You can't retrofit that extensibility after the fact, not on a government timeline. It has to be a decision made before the first contract: is the boundary between "my orchestration logic" and "the platform I'm orchestrating" narrow, versioned, and well-documented — or is it whatever got the pilot working fastest? The former costs more up front and looks identical in the pilot demo. It's also the only version that survives the jump from single-program funding to enterprise-wide funding without a full re-architecture in between. I've sat across the table from small autonomy companies working through exactly that tradeoff — whether to optimize for the current SBIR deliverable or for the interface that has to survive three more customers after it. It's rarely obvious in the moment which one you're doing. Worth deciding on purpose rather than by default. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy
author: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. • Отслеживаете
